newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai PM avenges humiliation with election call.
newsitem.headline: Thai PM avenges humiliation with election call.

text.p: Thailand's premier avenged his recent political humuliation by estranged coalition allies on Friday by calling fresh elections, but may have committed political suicide by doing so, analysts said.
Having been forced by key allies to declare last Saturday that he would quit within seven days, Banharn Silpa-archa made them sweat for nearly a week before pulling the rug from under their feet.

He allowed a political stalemate to fester by refusing to name his successor or attend coalition meetings. Then, in a surprise move, drove them them all out of office by calling fresh elections for November 17.
Chaiwat Kamchu, political scientist at Chulalongkorn Univeristy, said Banharn had taken his revenge on Defence Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, who had mastered the failed attempt to oust Banharn.
"In a way, this is revenge by Banharn, as he did not seem to want Chavalit to be the next prime minister," he said.
But Banharn still risked being defeated by his major rivals, the main opposition Democrat Party, in the coming election, Chaiwat added.
Banharn's six-party administration had been unpopular during its 14 months in power and was accused of condoning corruption and mismanaging the slowing economy.
His coalition controlled 209 of the 391 seats in parliament.
"In this election, the Democrats seem to have an advantage. They won more popularity during last week's no-confident debate against Banharn," he said.
"On the other hand, Chart Thai could become even more factionalized after Banharn's decision, which many in the party might view as unpopular," Chaiwat added.

At his Chart Thai party meeting, Banharn had especially accused Chavalit of double crossing him. He said Chavalit, who leads the coalition's second largest party, the New Aspiration Party (NAP), had pressured him to resign in exchange for support at a parliamentary no-confidence vote against him.
Banharn won the vote but vowed revenge.
"Those who have done bad things to others can't go to the top," Kanchana Silpa-archa, Banharn's member of paliament daughter, told a newspaper this week, apparently referring to Chavalit.

"Banharn made a very selfish move when he dissolved the house while the coalition partners were in a disadvantaged position," Chavalit's secretary Bunjong Veesommai told reporters after Banharn's announcement.
Banharn did not say whether he would run in the coming election. He also said he was unsure how his party would fare in the polls. "I cannot predict the turn out for the party," he told reporters.
"The Democrat Party looks set to take all the advantage from Banharn's political suicide of dissolving the house," Thawil Praison of the former coalition partner Palang Dharma Party told Reuters.

He said Banharn's Chart Thai party risked defeat in the upcoming election because many of its members would defect to other parties. "The chances of Banharn returning to power after the upcoming election is slim," he said.
Opposition leader Chuan Leekpai's Democrat Party won 86 seats in last July's election, second only to the Chart Thai party's 92, and has high ratings in local polls.

"Banharn, by dissolving parliament, risks the disintegration of his own party," said political analyst Sukhum Naulsakul. "The trend seems to be that the Democrat party would win the most seats in the upcoming election."
Other analysts welcomed the dissolution and said it showed the fledgling democracy in Thailand, which has seen 17 military coups or coup attempts since 1932, was developing well.
